fit: measured dried fig constituent and severe deficiency treatment case
assessment: Case 2 had a low serum magnesium concentration, cerebellar edema and delirium with visual hallucinations. Overall symptoms improved after intravenous magnesium, withdrawal of antiviral medication and prior thiamine treatment. Later low magnesium recurred with ataxia and no reported cognitive symptoms. Dried figs contain measured magnesium, but the case has no Parkinson diagnosis, food exposure or separately timed episode frequency.

fit: early Parkinson psychosis scales, visual subtype and frequency limitations
assessment: The original reports any psychotic features in 27 of 70 early Parkinson participants and three of 74 controls. The 10PDQ identifies sensory type separately from frequency of the worst psychotic experience, and CAARMS scores combine frequency and duration. The study does not track dried fig intake or separately count visual episodes after meals.

fit: robot-induced sense of presence in Parkinson disease
assessment: Conflicting sensorimotor stimulation examines sensed presence among different Parkinson symptom groups. In the four phantom-boarder cases, three reported complex visual hallucinations, separately from phantom-boarder episodes. The experiment neither changes food intake nor records visual episodes after dried figs.

fit: nigrostriatal uptake and visual hallucination status
assessment: The DLB and mild cognitive impairment imaging analysis relates lower regional dopamine transporter uptake to recorded hallucination status and other clinical features. Association with occurrence is distinct from change in episode frequency after eating, and food exposure is not measured.

fit: plasma biomarkers and presence of core DLB features
assessment: The investigators assay 172 baseline plasma samples, with repeated samples in 55. The second recruitment cohort uses the previously reported cardiac MIBG method, and a prior p-tau181 result is reused. Visual hallucinations are rated as present or absent for clinical classification, without a dried fig exposure.

fit: caregiver-rated NPI profiles across clinical diagnoses
assessment: The clinical comparison includes Parkinson disease with cognitive impairment, Alzheimer disease and frontotemporal dementia. It relates Neuropsychiatric Inventory outcomes to caregiver distress and other clinical variables. Those domain ratings are separate from counted visual episodes after eating dried figs.

fit: timing of visual hallucinations and combined electrolyte abnormalities
assessment: The original case describes a sudden, hours-long episode of visual hallucinations with severe hypomagnesemia and hypocalcemia. The case presentation says the hallucinations had already resolved when blood tests were ordered the following day. Later overall symptoms resolved during magnesium and active vitamin D treatment. Distinguish the first visual episode from general improvement during the admission. The patient had no reported Parkinson diagnosis and no documented dried fig exposure.

fit: visual hallucination onset after initial correction in severe magnesium depletion case
assessment: The patient entered hospital with very low serum magnesium and coexisting electrolyte abnormalities. Visual hallucinations first appeared after extubation, when measured serum magnesium had risen to 2.2 mg/dL. They persisted during further correction and oral supplementation, then were absent the day after quetiapine and melatonin were added. Multiple therapies and the changing critical-care state preclude attributing the visual course to magnesium alone. There is no Parkinson or dried fig comparison.

fit: reported dietary magnesium and prevalence of Parkinson disease
assessment: This NHANES analysis includes 20,010 adults over 40, 240 with Parkinson disease. The adjusted magnesium depletion score association is an odds ratio of 1.47 per unit (95% CI 1.16–1.86). The authors report insufficient evidence for a clear association between dietary magnesium intake and Parkinson disease in the main intake analysis, and describe a nonlinear model separately. The study compares recorded disease status, with no visual hallucination outcome or isolated dried fig exposure. The first online date precedes the July 2025 issue.

fit: primary cholinergic PET case-control comparison and visual symptom presence
assessment: The imaging report compares 25 newly diagnosed dementia with Lewy bodies participants, 15 Parkinson participants and 15 healthy controls. The visual hallucination interview is used to record presence or absence. In the dementia with Lewy bodies group, voxel-wise analyses do not find a clear relationship between tracer uptake and hallucination presence. This is the same study discussed in the commentary at PMC10473551. It has no dried fig exposure or food-timed clinical episode-rate measure.

fit: TOLEDO medication trial, visual adverse-event reports and ascertainment
assessment: Of 107 randomized participants, 106 entered the efficacy analysis, 53 in each group. TOLEDO's main endpoint was daily off time, not recurrent visual hallucinations. The report lists two hallucination adverse-event cases in each arm in the neuropsychiatric summary and separately lists a visual hallucination withdrawal during apomorphine treatment. These counts should not be added without an event-level linkage. Moderate psychosis was excluded, while very mild visual phenomena with insight were allowed. The trial is NCT02006121, distinct from the registered refractory visual hallucination study NCT02702076.

fit: refractory visual hallucination trial eligibility and severity outcomes
assessment: The US and EU registries identify the same proposed drug comparison. Eligibility requires visual hallucinations more than three times per week and primary assessment concerns a global severity score after four weeks. The registry does not supply measured results or a culinary exposure. This study is separate from TOLEDO.
